briefing.text: Whether a pathway is 'significantly mutated' is a statistical question. The percent of samples with any pathway mutation does not answer it, because large gene sets made of long genes get hit by chance. Count the samples with at least one nonsilent mutation in the pathway genes and compare that count with a null model that accounts for each sample's mutation count and each gene's coding length (for example, permute each sample's mutations across genes weighted by CDS length, or run per-sample binomial tests and combine them PathScan-style). Make the call from the null-model p-value. A high raw frequency with p>0.05 does not contradict 'not significantly mutated'.
briefing.reason: This sets the evidence standard for the label. Without it, a team could read a high raw mutation frequency as significance.

briefing.text: The result depends heavily on which genes define ERBB-PI3K. Write the gene list out. Use a narrow curated set as the primary test: EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PTEN, AKT1, AKT2, AKT3, MTOR, TSC1, TSC2, RICTOR, RPTOR, STK11, INPP4B and PPP2R1A, which is the TCGA 2018 PI3K set plus the ERBB receptors. Then rerun with a broader KEGG ErbB set as a sensitivity check. If the two disagree, report the curated result as primary and note the difference.
briefing.reason: How the gene set is defined can flip the conclusion, so it needs to be fixed in advance and checked for sensitivity.

briefing.text: Count only nonsilent coding variants as pathway hits: Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift, In_Frame, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site and Nonstop (check the Variant_Classification column in data_mutations.txt). Leave out silent, intronic, UTR, flank and other non-coding variants. Silent variants can be used to estimate the background rate.
briefing.reason: Including non-coding or silent variants inflates the number of pathway hits.

briefing.text: data_mutations.txt has a FILTER column (with values such as 'common_variant') and population-frequency columns (ExAC_AF, GMAF). Leftover germline polymorphisms, which are common in Asian-ancestry cohorts that reference panels cover poorly, can look like recurrent pathway mutations. Exclude calls flagged common_variant and calls with population AF above 1% (including ExAC_AF_EAS). Be wary of variants that recur at the same position in many samples but are not known hotspots. Rerun the test after filtering.
briefing.reason: Germline artefacts can make the pathway look falsely significant.

briefing.text: Sample IDs do not match between tables: the clinical table uses IDs like 'NPC15F' while Tumor_Sample_Barcode in the MAF uses IDs like 'NPC015D'. Compare the two ID sets and normalise the formats. Use all sequenced samples in data_clinical_sample.txt as the denominator, including any with zero mutations, not only the samples that appear in the MAF.
briefing.reason: A naive join drops samples and changes the denominator for frequency and significance.

briefing.text: Check whether any patient has more than one sample (compare unique PATIENT_ID with SAMPLE_ID, and look for suffixes that mark repeat samples). If so, keep one sample per patient before testing the pathway.
briefing.reason: Counting repeat samples from the same patient inflates recurrence.

briefing.text: One or a few hypermutated tumours can carry most of the pathway mutations. Look at mutations per sample (and TMB if it is available) and at what share of pathway hits comes from the top 1-3 samples. Count samples mutated rather than total mutations, use a per-sample null, or report the result with hypermutators excluded.
briefing.reason: Hypermutators can drive a false significant result.

briefing.text: The only molecular data here are point mutations and indels; there is no copy-number file. Published ERBB-PI3K alteration rates often include amplifications, which these data cannot show. Frame the test as mutation-level significance. Mutation data are enough to test 'significantly mutated', so a missing CNA file is not by itself grounds for 'Not verifiable'.
briefing.reason: This prevents a wrong 'Not verifiable' call and stops teams comparing these data with published rates that include copy-number alterations.

briefing.text: Record how many pathway or gene-set tests you run. If you test several, apply Benjamini-Hochberg and treat ERBB-PI3K as significant only if q<0.05. If it is the single pre-specified test, use p<0.05. Fisher-combined p-values are anti-conservative when their inputs are correlated.

referee.difference: Both teams use the same filtering, the same samples and the same length- and burden-weighted exome null, and both get the same numbers. They differ only in how they read 'ERBB-PI3K pathway'. X takes the narrow ERBB+PI3K/AKT/mTOR set without RAS as primary: 5/56, p~0.1, so True. Y includes KRAS/NRAS/HRAS (KEGG ErbB, RAS->PI3K) and adds hotspot evidence: 7/56, p~0.015, so False.
referee.test: Re-ran the PathScan-style Poisson-binomial null independently (referee_test.py) with fixed RefSeq CDS lengths. Grid: narrow vs narrow+RAS sets, exome 30 or 35 Mb, with or without hypermutator NPC15F. The question was whether either set's verdict is robust across the nuisance choices, or whether one side's result is an artefact of a nuisance setting. Also tried a length-free selection test (nonsilent:silent ratio, and the MAF Hotspot flag in pathway vs background).
referee.expected_if_x: If X is right, the excess is not robust: the RAS-inclusive set's significance disappears under some reasonable nuisance setting, or the narrow set is clearly null, and the length-free selection tests show no pathway enrichment.
referee.expected_if_y: If Y is right, the pathway excess holds across nuisance settings, and the length-free tests show selection.
referee.outcome: Narrow set: 5/56, p=0.16/0.09 at 30 Mb and 0.10/0.056 at 35 Mb (with/without hypermutator). It is never below 0.05, but it is consistently borderline. Narrow+RAS: 7/56, p=0.023/0.010 at 30 Mb and 0.011/0.004 at 35 Mb, significant under every setting. So neither result is a nuisance artefact; the verdict flips only on whether RAS is included. The length-free tests were uninformative: the MAF has only 4 silent calls, and the Hotspot column is 0 for every call.
referee.reason: Both computations are correct and reproducible. The disagreement is a reading of 'ERBB-PI3K pathway' (with or without RAS), and the data cannot arbitrate that. My answer.json leans False because the canonical KEGG ErbB pathway includes RAS and RAS directly activates PI3K, but that is a reading choice, not a test result.

findings.question: In pathway-level significance tests for somatic mutations (e.g. PathScan, MutSig-style or gene-set permutation approaches), how should the background gene universe and gene-length/coverage be handled when the mutation file contains only a filtered subset of genes, and how do the results differ between a length-weighted per-sample null and an unweighted random gene-set null?
findings.answer: PathScan's null is built on gene length: under random mutation, longer genes are more likely to be hit. It computes a per-sample probability that the pathway is mutated given that sample's mutation burden, then combines samples using Fisher-Lancaster. MutSigCV also defines significance against a background rate per covered base, per gene and per patient, and assumes full coverage when no coverage file is given. The background universe should therefore be all sequenced genes, i.e. the whole exome weighted by CDS length, not only the genes that appear in a filtered MAF. Shrinking the universe to MAF genes inflates the pathway's share and makes the p-value unstable. An unweighted random gene-set null ignores both gene length and per-sample burden, so the length-weighted per-sample (PathScan-style) null is the valid choice. No source gives a recipe for a filtered MAF; that part is my inference from how the methods are defined.

findings.question: In standard curated pathway definitions (e.g. TCGA 2018 oncogenic signaling pathways, KEGG ErbB), are RAS genes (KRAS/HRAS/NRAS) considered part of the 'ERBB-PI3K' signaling pathway or a separate RTK-RAS pathway?
findings.answer: The TCGA 2018 curation (Sanchez-Vega et al.) treats PI3K/Akt and RTK-RAS as two separate pathways. KRAS, NRAS and HRAS belong to RTK-RAS, together with EGFR, ERBB2-4, BRAF and NF1. KEGG hsa04012 (ErbB signaling) does include a RAS-ERK branch (element N00021, EGF-ERBB2-RAS-ERK) alongside its PI3K branch. A label like 'ERBB-PI3K' most naturally means the ERBB receptors plus the PI3K axis, without RAS. Including RAS follows the broader KEGG ErbB convention. Run both as a sensitivity check. The truncated page text did not show the full gene tables, so the RAS placement in TCGA rests on the figure text and the pathway list.

findings.question: Does the presence of known activating hotspot mutations in a few samples constitute evidence that a pathway is 'significantly mutated' in the statistical sense used by cancer-genomics studies, or is that term reserved for a frequency-versus-background test?
findings.answer: In cancer genomics, 'significantly mutated' is a statistical term. It means a gene or pathway is mutated more often than chance would predict under a background mutation model (as in MutSigCV and PathScan), with FDR control. Known hotspots in a few samples show functional or driver relevance, which is how TCGA 2018 counts OncoKB-curated alterations, but they are not on their own evidence of statistical significance. Hotspot or clustering evidence counts only when it is part of a test against a background.
